1. A vibration device for bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the vibration device comprising:

a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side;

a vibration motor coupled to the first side;

a perimeter member extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, the perimeter member being rigid and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face of a low-friction material, the chamber being bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and, when the bearing face is placed in contact with an exposed face of the covering element, by the exposed face, and a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber; and

an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber, the air-extraction mechanism being operable to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while the ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, a resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device against the covering element;

wherein a vibration transmission path from the vibration motor to the bearing face passes through the base and the perimeter member, each member of the vibration transmission path is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

wherein the bearing face is slidable over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained.

2. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the perimeter member is a closed loop that runs around the chamber at a perimeter of the second side.

3. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the low-friction material of the bearing face is plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

4. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the perimeter member is free of rubber, elastomer and foam, and makes rigid contact with the exposed face.

5. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the pressure differential produces a holding force sufficient to hold the vibration device against the exposed face without a downward force being applied by an operator.

6. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the air-extraction mechanism is operable to withdraw air from the chamber continuously while the vibration motor operates.

7. The vibration device of claim 1, wherein the air-extraction mechanism is a vacuum pump.

8. The vibration device of claim 1, further comprising a handle arranged to guide the vibration device over the exposed face while the pressure differential holds the vibration device against the covering element.

9. The vibration device of claim 1, further comprising a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device, the vibration device being translatable over the exposed face by tension applied to the flexible pulling element while the pressure differential is maintained.

10. A system for bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the system comprising:

a vibration device comprising a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side, a vibration motor coupled to the first side, a perimeter member extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side, and an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber,

the perimeter member being rigid and terminating, remote from the base, in a bearing face of a low-friction material, the chamber being bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and, when the bearing face is placed in contact with an exposed face of the covering element, by the exposed face, and a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face, through which clearance ambient air enters the chamber,

the air-extraction mechanism being operable to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while the ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, a resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device against the covering element,

and a vibration transmission path from the vibration motor to the bearing face passing through the base and the perimeter member, each member of the vibration transmission path being rigid and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount being interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device, the flexible pulling element being incapable of transmitting compression to the vibration device and being arranged to move the vibration device across the exposed face when tension is applied to it,

whereby a position of the vibration device over the exposed face is controlled by tension applied to the flexible pulling element while a force holding the vibration device against the covering element is supplied independently of the flexible pulling element by the pressure differential.

11. The system of claim 10, wherein the flexible pulling element is a rope, a wire or a cable.

12. The system of claim 10, wherein the low-friction material of the bearing face is plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

13. The system of claim 10, wherein the perimeter member is free of rubber, elastomer and foam, and wherein the pressure differential produces a holding force sufficient to hold the vibration device against the exposed face without a downward force being applied by an operator.

14. A method of bedding a covering element into a bonding material, the method comprising:

placing a vibration device on an exposed face of the covering element that has been laid on the bonding material, the vibration device comprising a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side, a vibration motor coupled to the first side, a rigid perimeter member extending from the second side and surrounding a chamber located on the second side and terminating in a bearing face of a low-friction material, and an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber, whereby the bearing face is brought into contact with the exposed face so that the chamber is bounded by the second side, the perimeter member and the exposed face, with a clearance remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member, between the bearing face and the exposed face;

operating the air-extraction mechanism to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, and holding the vibration device against the covering element by a resulting pressure differential;

operating the vibration motor and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor to the covering element along a vibration transmission path passing through the base, the perimeter member and the bearing face, each member of the vibration transmission path being rigid and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount being interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

translating the vibration device across the exposed face, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face over the exposed face, so that the vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element.

15. The method of claim 14, wherein the pressure differential is maintained continuously while the vibration device is translated across the exposed face, so that the vibration device is held against the covering element and slid over the exposed face at the same time.

16. The method of claim 14, wherein the vibration device is translated across the exposed face by applying tension to a flexible pulling element connected to the vibration device.

17. The method of claim 14, wherein the vibration device is translated across the exposed face by guiding the vibration device with a handle, and wherein no downward force is applied to the vibration device by an operator while the vibration motor operates.

18. The method of claim 14, wherein the low-friction material of the bearing face is polytetrafluoroethylene.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
<!-- Abstract - body text only, no heading line. -->

A vibration device for bedding covering elements into thinset, mortar or adhesive has a rigid base carrying a vibration motor and an air-extraction mechanism on its first side and a chamber on its second side. A rigid perimeter member surrounds the chamber and ends in a bearing face of low-friction material such as plastic or PTFE. It is not a seal: a clearance remains against the exposed face of the covering element, and ambient air enters the chamber continuously. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air fast enough to keep the chamber below atmospheric pressure while air keeps entering, and the pressure differential presses the device onto the covering element without downward force from the operator. Every member between the motor and the covering element is rigid, so vibration transfers with little damping, and the bearing face lets the device slide to successive areas without releasing the hold.

content.content:
1	When a tile, slab or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.
2	
3	Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place.
4	
5	Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.
6	
7	The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles reduce some of the vibration reaching the operator, but they do so by absorbing mechanical energy that would otherwise have gone into the covering element, so the tool is made kinder to the operator by being made worse at its job. The two problems are coupled: firmer coupling to the covering element is obtained by pressing harder, and pressing harder is exactly what increases the vibration dose to the operator.
8	
9	What is needed is a way to hold a vibration device against a covering element with a force that does not come from the operator's arms, to conduct the vibration into the covering element without passing it through any compliant member, and to allow the device to be moved from area to area over the covering element without ever giving up that hold.

When a tile, slab or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.

Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place.

Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.

The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles reduce some of the vibration reaching the operator, but they do so by absorbing mechanical energy that would otherwise have gone into the covering element, so the tool is made kinder to the operator by being made worse at its job. The two problems are coupled: firmer coupling to the covering element is obtained by pressing harder, and pressing harder is exactly what increases the vibration dose to the operator.

What is needed is a way to hold a vibration device against a covering element with a force that does not come from the operator's arms, to conduct the vibration into the covering element without passing it through any compliant member, and to allow the device to be moved from area to area over the covering element without ever giving up that hold.

content.content:
1	A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and its bearing face is of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.
2	
3	The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.
4	
5	Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator does not have to press the device against the covering element and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is removed rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base, the perimeter member and the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element without being absorbed on the way. The device is thus coupled harder and held down harder than a pressed-on sliding base, while the operator's hands carry less.
6	
7	Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.
8	
9	In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.
10	
11	A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.
12

A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and its bearing face is of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials.

The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.

Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator does not have to press the device against the covering element and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is removed rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base, the perimeter member and the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element without being absorbed on the way. The device is thus coupled harder and held down harder than a pressed-on sliding base, while the operator's hands carry less.

Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.

In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.

A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.

# FIG. 5 - Second embodiment with a pulling element

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left, as FIG. 1 but from further off, so several laid tiles are in frame. Outline line work, no shading or hatching. The sheet contains only the parts listed. No word, letter, digit or label appears, and no border.

**Geometry to be drawn**

- The covering element 36 is a flat floor of a few large square tiles in perspective filling the lower part of the sheet, joined edge to edge in one plane with a straight joint line between neighbours. The floor is otherwise plain. The tile at the lower right of the sheet is drawn large and is left entirely bare: nothing stands on it and no line crosses it, so its whole surface is one broad unbroken stretch of plain tile. That tile surface is part of the covering element itself. Identified well inside that bare tile surface at the lower right, clear of the joint lines that bound it and clear of every other body on the sheet.
- The vibration device 10 is a shallow rectangular assembly standing on a tile farther back in the view, above the bare tile at the lower right and not on it, drawn as on FIG. 1: a flat slab carrying a rectangular motor housing at its left end, a rectangular pump housing standing on the slab to the right of that housing, and a grip standing on the slab at its right end, the three bodies touching one another nowhere. The whole assembly is drawn with one continuous outer silhouette. Identified on that continuous outer silhouette.
- The flexible pulling element 46 is the one slack cord on the sheet, drawn as a single curved path of even thickness and the only curving element on the sheet. The path runs from the left end of the slab away to the left, sags gently, and passes off the left edge of the sheet in one unbroken sweep, without doubling back or crossing itself. It lies over the floor, so the path is unbroken along its whole length and passes in front of any joint line it meets, that joint line stopping at the side of the path and starting again beyond it. Identified on that curved path where it runs over the floor clear of the slab.

I applied the full source-fidelity strip the reviewer required, across the claims, description, numeral table, drawing descriptions, and all five figure briefs.

**Removed as untraceable to the disclosure:** the separate PTFE facing, the through-base extraction opening, the duct/support column, motor fasteners and direct fastened mounting, the exhaust outlet, the no-valve limitation, the electrical supply with cord and battery alternatives, the integral one-piece loop and fastened perimeter joint, the attachment formation and its low placement, plural chambers and dividing walls, vertical/wall use, the particulate separator, the quantitative pump-selection and settling-point doctrine, the treatment end point and shut-down sequence, the bail-handle geometry and lift-and-carry function, the loop plan geometry and single-plane bearing face, the base material and section variants, the motor-type list, the fan/blower/ejector alternatives, the bearing-face width design rule, the self-restoring/lippage narrative, the covering-element and substrate enumerations, the in-plane pulling-force limitation, operator stance and working distance, and the spreading/laying method steps.

1	In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.
2	
3	Overview
4	
5	FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 show a vibration device 10 in use, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material that is plastic when the covering element 36 is laid and hardens afterwards. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the proportion of the underside of the covering element 36 that is wetted by the bonding material 40, and improves the contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40.
6	
7	The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.
8	
9	The base
10	
11	The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.
12	
13	The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.
14	
15	The vibration motor
16	
17	The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no resilient mount, rubber bush or foam pad interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.
18	
19	The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.
20	
21	The air-extraction mechanism
22	
23	The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.
24	
25	The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.
26	
27	The perimeter member and the chamber
28	
29	A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 near its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The joint between the perimeter member 24 and the base 12 is rigid and carries vibration across itself without loss.
30	
31	The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member.
32	
33	The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.
34	
35	Because the perimeter member 24 is rigid and the exposed face 38 is neither perfectly flat nor perfectly clean, in that it carries dust, grains of bonding material 40 and its own surface texture, and the covering element 36 itself may be slightly bowed, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale, and so are the departures from flatness of the exposed face 38 that give rise to it. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22, and does so by presenting a long, narrow, high-resistance path around the whole loop, without closing that path.
36	
37	The pressure differential that holds the device down
38	
39	The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.
40	
41	The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.
42	
43	A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.
44	
45	The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and slides under the holding force with a modest in-plane resistance, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No mode has to be switched, no air cushion has to be raised under the device, and no grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36 at full amplitude, instead of falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.
46	
47	The vibration transmission path
48	
49	The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 through the rigid joint at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.
50	
51	The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38 throughout each vibration cycle. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area and from one operator to the next.
52	
53	The clearance 34 does not stand between the bearing face 26 and the covering element 36 in the way that a film of air stands between a pressed-on sliding base and the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film, being compressible, both stores and dissipates part of what crosses it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 is a leakage path in parallel with the contact rather than a compliant layer in series with it: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.
54	
55	The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because the operator applies no downward force, there is no loaded path from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.
56	
57	Handles
58	
59	One or more handles 44 may be coupled to the base 12. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and it need not be dimensioned or damped as though it were, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.
60	
61	Embodiment with a flexible pulling element
62	
63	FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.
64	
65	This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 can transmit force only along its own length and, being flexible, cannot transmit compression at all. It therefore cannot press the vibration device 10 down against the covering element 36, whatever the operator does with it. The flexible pulling element 46 is thus incapable of transmitting compression to the vibration device 10, and moves it across the exposed face 38 when tension is applied. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.
66	
67	Method of use
68	
69	A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought into contact with the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without downward force applied by an operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.
70

In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.

Overview

FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 show a vibration device 10 in use, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material that is plastic when the covering element 36 is laid and hardens afterwards. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the proportion of the underside of the covering element 36 that is wetted by the bonding material 40, and improves the contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40.

The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.

The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 does not deflect enough to absorb an appreciable fraction of the vibration energy, and it transmits that energy to the perimeter member 24 substantially undiminished.

The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22, and the chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.

The vibration motor

The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no resilient mount, rubber bush or foam pad interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.

The vibration motor 18 may be of any type that produces mechanical vibration in the base 12. What matters to the arrangement described here is not the mechanism by which the vibration is generated but the path by which it leaves the vibration device 10, which is dealt with below.

The air-extraction mechanism

The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12 and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.

The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.

The perimeter member and the chamber

A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 near its perimeter. In the embodiment of FIG. 3 the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The joint between the perimeter member 24 and the base 12 is rigid and carries vibration across itself without loss.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The bearing face 26 is a low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is rigid and the exposed face 38 is neither perfectly flat nor perfectly clean, in that it carries dust, grains of bonding material 40 and its own surface texture, and the covering element 36 itself may be slightly bowed, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale, and so are the departures from flatness of the exposed face 38 that give rise to it. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22, and does so by presenting a long, narrow, high-resistance path around the whole loop, without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.

A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and slides under the holding force with a modest in-plane resistance, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No mode has to be switched, no air cushion has to be raised under the device, and no grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36 at full amplitude, instead of falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 through the rigid joint at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38 throughout each vibration cycle. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area and from one operator to the next.

The clearance 34 does not stand between the bearing face 26 and the covering element 36 in the way that a film of air stands between a pressed-on sliding base and the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film, being compressible, both stores and dissipates part of what crosses it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 is a leakage path in parallel with the contact rather than a compliant layer in series with it: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the only force the operator supplies is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because the operator applies no downward force, there is no loaded path from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

One or more handles 44 may be coupled to the base 12. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. It is not used to press the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36, and it need not be dimensioned or damped as though it were, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 can transmit force only along its own length and, being flexible, cannot transmit compression at all. It therefore cannot press the vibration device 10 down against the covering element 36, whatever the operator does with it. The flexible pulling element 46 is thus incapable of transmitting compression to the vibration device 10, and moves it across the exposed face 38 when tension is applied. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought into contact with the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without downward force applied by an operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12, the perimeter member 24 and the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 is a leakage path in parallel with the contact rather than a compliant layer in series with it: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

a base that is rigid and has a first side and a second side opposite the first side;

an air-extraction mechanism coupled to the first side and in fluid communication with the chamber, the air-extraction mechanism being operable to withdraw air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while the ambient air continues to enter the chamber through the clearance, a resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device against the covering element;

wherein a vibration transmission path from the vibration motor to the bearing face passes through the base and the perimeter member, each member of the vibration transmission path is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed in the vibration transmission path; and

wherein the bearing face is slidable over the exposed face while the pressure differential is maintained.

33	The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.
34	
35	Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.
36	
37	The pressure differential that holds the device down
38	
39	The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.
40	
41	The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.
42	
43	A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.
44	
45	The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.
46	
47	The vibration transmission path
48	
49	The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 through the rigid joint at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.
50	
51	The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38 throughout each vibration cycle. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.
52	
53	The clearance 34 does not stand between the bearing face 26 and the covering element 36 in the way that a film of air stands between a pressed-on sliding base and the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 admits air into the chamber 22 alongside the contact rather than lying between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.
54

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of a perimeter member 24 of the general kind shown in FIG. 2, taken at a place along the loop where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is far too small to be drawn to scale. FIG. 2 accordingly shows the perimeter member 24 resting on the covering element 36 without any gap, at the scale of that view, and the clearance 34 appears only in the enlarged detail of FIG. 4, where it is drawn many times its true height. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. In use the operator's hands carry no part of the contact load.

A property of this arrangement should be noted, because it is what the arrangement is for.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 through the rigid joint at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38 throughout each vibration cycle. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not stand between the bearing face 26 and the covering element 36 in the way that a film of air stands between a pressed-on sliding base and the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and makes hard, direct contact with it over the remainder of the loop, and it is that contact, not the clearance 34, that carries the vibration. The clearance 34 admits air into the chamber 22 alongside the contact rather than lying between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38: air passes along it, edgewise, into the chamber 22, and the vibration passes across the contact beside it. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

59	The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and does not vary with how, how hard, or from what angle the operator pulls.

input.summary: Applied every listed finding. Six passages of untraced technical substance were removed or replaced with disclosure-grounded wording in the detailed description, the "incapable of transmitting compression" limitation was struck from claim 10 and the description, and the four drawing contradictions were resolved: FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 now show the perimeter member as the member touching the tile, FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 no longer negate a route through the base, FIG. 3 places the loop at the perimeter as two nested rectangles, and numeral 36 now means the single tile the device stands on across all sheets.
reasoning: The untraced explanatory material in the description was cut to what the disclosure actually says. The cause of the clearance is now the disclosed fact that the perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, rather than invented surface-condition and flatness facts. The restriction mechanism is now simply that the perimeter member restricts the flow without closing the path, with no length, width or resistance characterization. The bonding material is named without a cure property. The sliding paragraph drops the quantified resistance, the air-cushion comparison and the full-amplitude absolute, keeping the disclosed contrast that intensity no longer falls away with distance from a fixed attachment point. The consistency claim ends at the working area. The interface paragraph keeps the disclosed damping statement and describes the clearance as admitting air alongside the contact rather than lying between the faces, dropping the parallel/series model and the energy-storage assertion.

Claim 10 lost its negative capability limitation. What now distinguishes the system claim is the decoupled-control relationship that the disclosure states affirmatively: position is set by tension on the flexible pulling element while the holding force is supplied independently and continuously by the pressure differential. That relationship, together with the non-sealing rigid perimeter and the all-rigid transmission path carried into the claim body, is what the claim rests on. The description paragraph was reduced in the same way, so claim and description use the same words.

The FIG. 1 defect was the most serious drawing finding, because the sole in-use perspective showed the base sitting on the tile with the only member that actually touches the tile invisible. FIG. 1 now carries the perimeter member 24 as a shallow band running round the underside of the slab at its edge, holding the slab clear of the tile, and the base's front band is described with the perimeter member below it and plain tile below that. Numeral 24 is on the sheet, six numerals in total, within the cap. I made the same correction in FIG. 5 and numbered the band there too, so no depicted body is left unidentified.

The through-base negation was a contradiction between the briefs and the claims, not a missing structure. Since the corrective turn removed the extraction opening and duct as unsupported, the repair is silence rather than an added route: FIG. 2 no longer says the slab has no opening anywhere, FIG. 3 no longer says no shape appears inside the loop, both briefs state that the route of communication is not depicted in that view, and the Brief Description of FIG. 2 says the same. Nothing was added to the invention to excuse the drawing.

FIG. 3 was reduced from three nested rectangles to two, so the outer edge of the loop coincides with the outline of the underside of the plate.
